Chapter 9: Applying Attachment Principles in Friendships and Work
We usually hear about attachment theory in the context of romantic partners or family, right? But here’s the thing—those same core needs for security, acceptance, and a reliable connection? They show up everywhere in our lives, especially in our friendships and at work.
Think about your closest friends. Maybe you notice you tend to pour a lot of energy into those relationships. Or sometimes, you pull back and keep a little distance. Some folks are able to keep things balanced, where the give and take feels just right. Understanding your own patterns can help you pick friends who truly support your growth—and it makes setting healthy boundaries a whole lot easier.
Here are a few ways you can use attachment principles to strengthen your friendships:
First, choose friends who are consistent and trustworthy. After you spend time together, check in with yourself. Do you feel energized, or maybe a bit drained or anxious?
Next, don’t be afraid to communicate your needs and limits. It’s perfectly okay to ask for help—or to say no if you’re feeling overwhelmed.
And when misunderstandings happen—and let’s face it, they will—try to repair things directly instead of letting resentment build up. A little honesty can go a long way.
Now, let’s talk about the workplace. Attachment needs play a big role in how we relate to colleagues, supervisors, and even entire teams.
For example, if you tend to feel anxious, you might find yourself looking for lots of feedback or worrying about being left out. If you lean more avoidant, you might prefer working alone and try to minimize group projects.
So, how can you use attachment awareness to boost your professional relationships?
Start by seeking clarity in your communication. Be open about your expectations, and ask for feedback in a straightforward, respectful way.
Building trust is key, too. That means following through on your commitments—and owning up to mistakes when they happen.
Finally, try to foster a supportive environment. Encourage open dialogue and appreciate the different ways people like to work. A little understanding creates space for everyone to thrive.
When you take these attachment principles beyond just romance, you start to build a web of secure, supportive relationships that boost your well-being and resilience—no matter where you are or who you’re with.
